terms.name: Where to get character cards?
terms.desc: [[character]] cards in SillyTavern format are available on several community websites. [Chub.ai](https://chub.ai) (Character Hub) is the largest repository — search, preview, and download cards directly as .json files ready to import into Glaze. For characters from Janitor AI, use [datacat.run](https://datacat.run) to export any character as a card file — including private ones and those with proxy disabled. [Backyard.ai](https://backyard.ai) also has a library of cards you can download.

terms.name: Why is the model thinking inside the message?
terms.desc: The model is sending its reasoning (chain of thought) inside the response text rather than in a separate block. See [[preset-reasoning|Reasoning]] — enable 'Parse Inline Reasoning' to automatically extract thinking from tags like <think>...</think> and display it in a separate reasoning block.

terms.name: Where to find an LLM?
terms.desc: You need an [[api|API provider]] — a service that gives you access to AI models. After signing up, you'll get an API endpoint and key to enter in Glaze's API settings.

terms.name: The model is censoring my messages
terms.desc: Try a good preset — for example, fawnie from the built-in presets. Make sure to use at least inline CoT (the additional thinking feature in the preset). Note that censorship can also depend on the provider, even if the model is the same. It's not just the chat that matters — all data in the preset affects this, including your [[persona]] and [[character]] card. The model can be triggered by sexual descriptions in them.

terms.name: Which models should I use?
terms.desc: A few options for different tastes and budgets. Bang for the buck — DeepSeek V3.2. Middle ground — Gemini 3.1 Pro. Flagship model — Claude Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.6. For those tired of the rest — GLM 5.1. Others aren't really worth the attention — either because of poor context size or mediocre writing.

terms.name: “Compact history” says there is nothing to compact
terms.desc:
The button leaves the newest part of the chat alone: the latest messages within “Keep as written” (25% of the chat connection's context by default) stay as they are, and only what is older is retold. If the whole history fits in that amount, there is nothing to retell. With a large context (hundreds of thousands of tokens or more) this happens a lot.

What to do: lower “Keep as written” in the summary settings (say, to 10% or to a fixed 30–50 thousand tokens), or press “Compact all but the newest messages” right in the note. More in [[summary-compact|Manual compaction]].

terms.name: LLM
terms.desc: An AI that reads and writes text. It works by looking at your entire conversation and predicting what word comes next, one piece at a time. Examples: Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Deepseek V3.2.

terms.name: Token
terms.desc: The smallest piece of text the AI reads and writes — roughly 3/4 of a word. Every message you type and every reply you get is counted in tokens. There's also a limit: once the conversation is too long, the oldest messages get cut off. More tokens = higher cost and slower replies.

terms.name: Why token counts differ
terms.desc: Glaze counts [[token]]s locally, with the tokenizer of the model family the connection uses: OpenAI's o200k_base for GPT-4o and newer, and the published tokenizers of the other major families for their models. By default the connection's Tokenizer setting is Auto and picks the family from the model name (o200k_base when the name says nothing); you can also pick one by hand under Context Size. The Prompt Inspector shows which one counted. Each tokenizer is downloaded once, the first time it is needed (1–5 MB); until it arrives Glaze keeps counting with the previous one, or at about four characters per token on the very first launch. Claude 3 and newer and Gemini do not publish their exact tokenizers, so their counts stay an estimate for planning — expect a few percent of difference. For what you are actually charged, check your provider's own usage page.

terms.name: Context
terms.desc: The maximum amount of [[token]]s the AI can see at once — its working memory. Everything Glaze sends (system instructions, [[preset]] blocks, [[lorebook]] entries, chat history, and the new reply) must fit inside this window. When the conversation grows too long, older messages are trimmed to stay within the limit. Context Size is set in model settings and must not exceed the model's maximum.

terms.name: Context Size
terms.desc: A local Glaze setting — it is not sent to the provider. It caps how many [[token]]s the whole prompt may use. Glaze trims the chat, dropping the oldest messages, so the assembled prompt fits within this size before it is sent. Set it to match your model's [[context|context window]]; raising it above the model's real limit does not give the model more memory. When trimming chat history, Glaze takes the Context Size, subtracts [[max-tokens|Max Output Tokens]] from it (a provider requirement), and fits as many whole history messages as it can into the number that remains.

terms.name: History Trimming
terms.alt: In blocks, Continuous, History trim mode
terms.desc: How Glaze cuts the chat history once it no longer fits the [[context|context window]]. **Continuous** drops exactly what does not fit on every turn — always the most history, but the prompt starts at a different message each turn, so a provider's prompt cache rarely hits. **In blocks** holds the start of the history still and drops a whole block only when the whole prompt — as the prompt inspector counts it — gets past the trim trigger, a share of the context window. Between jumps the request begins with the same bytes, so a provider's prompt cache can hit: one big miss instead of one per turn. A turn whose lorebooks swell can cut the history deep; once they shrink back the start moves back to where a jump would have left it. **Pin cache anchor** in a message's menu (stepped trim mode only) starts the history at that message instead, until it no longer fits. The mode lives on the connection because it trades tokens for cache behaviour. See [[step-size]] and the trim group in the connection's Context section.

terms.name: Step Size
terms.desc: An **In blocks** setting: how much of the context window one jump frees when the prompt gets past the trim trigger. With a trigger of 85% and a step of 30%, a jump cuts the prompt back to 55% of the window, so the next turns have 30% of the window to grow into — and the prompt keeps the same start for as many turns as it takes to spend it. Bigger steps mean rarer jumps and longer runs where the prompt cache holds, at the cost of showing less history. A step larger than the room the history has above the preset, lorebooks and memory frees half of that room instead. Works together with the trim trigger (how full the prompt may get before a jump), both shares of the context window as the prompt inspector shows it.

terms.name: Max Output Tokens
terms.desc: A limit sent to the provider on how many [[token]]s the model may produce in a single reply. Generation stops the moment this limit is reached — even mid-sentence. The model does not see this value and does not plan its answer around it. It caps only the length of the reply; it does not reserve or affect the [[context|context window]].

terms.name: First-chunk Timeout
terms.desc: How long Glaze waits (in seconds) for the first piece of the reply to arrive after a request is sent. If nothing comes back within this time, the request is aborted instead of hanging on a stalled connection. Raise it for slow providers or very large prompts; lower it to fail faster.

terms.name: API
terms.desc: Typically a service that provides a special link — an endpoint — and a key to access it. Glaze connects to this endpoint to send your messages to the AI and receive replies. Must support the OpenAI-compatible format. Recommended providers: [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) and [LinkAPI](https://linkapi.ai).

terms.name: API Key
terms.desc: A secret code that proves you have permission to use an AI service. Never share it — anyone who has it can use the service as if they were you.

terms.name: Send preset instructions as system_instruction
terms.desc: When enabled, the run of `system` prompt blocks at the very start of the prompt is sent in a separate parameter: `system_instruction` on Google Gemini, `system` on Anthropic. Each block goes as its own part; they are not glued together. It does not touch the chat history itself — blocks inside it stay where they are and go as ordinary messages. Note that only a run at the start is lifted: if a `user` block comes first, nothing is.

terms.name: Exclude reasoning from the context limit
terms.desc: When [[preset-reasoning|reasoning]] is sent back to the provider, its tokens take up room in the [[context|context window]] and push out older messages. With this on they are still sent but not counted, so more history fits. Token counting is an estimate, so with long reasoning the request can overshoot the provider's real limit. Enable only if you accept that risk.

terms.name: Send session_id
terms.desc: Sends the provider a session number so the prompt cache stays warm. Requires a compatible provider. Leave it off if you are unsure.

terms.name: Streaming
terms.desc: When turned on, the AI sends its reply word by word as it writes — like watching someone type in real time. When turned off, you wait for the full reply before seeing anything. May provoke stronger censorship from the model. Recommended to disable.

terms.name: Chat Completion
terms.desc: The message format Glaze uses to talk to the AI: a list of messages, each labeled as 'system' (hidden instructions), 'user' (your messages), or 'assistant' (AI replies). Glaze assembles this list automatically from your [[preset]] blocks.

terms.name: Character
terms.desc: An AI character card — a description of who the AI is playing. Includes the character's name, personality, backstory, scenario, example dialogues, and avatar. A character can have multiple independent [[chat-session]]s, its own [[lorebook]] entries, and custom settings via [[connections]].

terms.name: Persona
terms.desc: Your in-app identity for the roleplay. A persona has a name, an avatar, and a prompt that describes who 'you' are in the story. The prompt is included in the AI's context. You can have multiple personas and assign different ones to different characters or chats.

terms.name: Chat Session
terms.desc: A separate conversation branch with a character. Each session has its own full message history, [[authornote]], and [[summary]]. You can create as many sessions as you like with the same character — for example, to explore different story paths without overwriting your existing chat.

terms.name: Connections
terms.desc: Links a [[lorebook]], [[preset]], or [[persona]] to a specific scope. Scopes: globally (all chats), per character, or per individual chat session. Priority: chat > character > global. Lets different characters or conversations automatically use different settings without manual switching.

terms.name: Character & Chats Hiding
terms.desc: Hiding a [[character]] removes it — and all of its [[chat-session]]s — from your Characters list, chat history, search, and filters. Nothing is deleted; the character is simply tucked away out of sight. To reveal hidden characters again, quickly tap the Characters tab 10 times in a row; tap it 10 more times to hide them again. The reveal is session-only and resets when you restart the app. The first time you hide a character, a one-time explainer describes how this works.

terms.name: Swipes
terms.desc: Multiple generated replies for the same message position. If you don't like the AI's reply, swipe or tap arrows to see another version. Only the version you land on is included in the conversation. You can also request a [[guided-swipe]] to steer the next attempt in a specific direction.

terms.name: Guided Generation
terms.desc: A [[swipes]] variant where you add a one-time instruction before regenerating. For example: 'make the scene more tense' or 'have the character mention the forest'. The instruction steers just this one generation. It is saved in the chat history for convenience, but is not sent to the AI in subsequent requests.

terms.name: Impersonation
terms.desc: Generate a reply as if you were your own character — useful for writing your side of the dialogue when you're not sure what to say. Uses a [[guided]] instruction block to tell the AI to write from your perspective instead of the character's.

terms.name: Selection Mode
terms.desc: Lets you select multiple messages at once for bulk deletion or hiding. Activate by long-pressing a message, then tap checkboxes on each message you want to include.

terms.name: Hidden Message
terms.desc: A message that is excluded from what gets sent to the AI but still visible in your chat. Useful for pruning old or unwanted messages to save space without permanently deleting them. Hidden messages appear faded with a small indicator. To hide a message, select it using [[selection-mode]].

terms.name: Chat Session
terms.desc: A separate conversation branch with a character. Each session has its own full message history, [[authornote]], and [[summary]]. You can create as many sessions as you like with the same character — for example, to explore different story paths without overwriting your existing chat.

terms.name: Connections
terms.desc: Links a [[lorebook]], [[preset]], or [[persona]] to a specific scope. Scopes: globally (all chats), per character, or per individual chat session. Priority: chat > character > global. Lets different characters or conversations automatically use different settings without manual switching.

terms.name: Quick Access
terms.desc: A side panel that slides in during a chat. All necessary chat settings are located here: [[character]] info, active [[lorebook]] entries, Author's Note, summary, sessions, preset, and persona settings. Open it with the wand button in the chat input area.

terms.name: Triggered Items
terms.desc: An icon [icon:triggered-items] that appears on a message when at least one [[lorebook]] entry or [[regex]] script was activated during its generation. Tap it to see exactly which lorebook entries were injected and which regex scripts were applied to that message.

terms.name: Request Preview
terms.desc: A very handy tool to debug your prompt. It shows the exact [[chatcompletion|JSON Chat Completion]] payload Glaze is sending to the [[api|API provider]]. It's useful for debugging prompt issues, seeing how [[macro]]s are expanded, and checking which [[lorebook]] entries and [[regex]] scripts are being injected. You can view the request both in a formatted view and as raw JSON.

terms.name: Image Generation
terms.desc: A background service that monitors messages for image generation tags (like `[IMG:GEN]`). When a tag is detected, it handles the API request to OpenAI, Google, or Naistera to generate an inline image directly in the chat. It can also send visual references — such as character avatars or your own custom images — to help the AI maintain consistency in the generated art.

terms.name: Preset
terms.desc: A customizable set of instructions Glaze sends to the AI before every reply. Made up of blocks you can turn on/off and reorder: System (global rules), Persona (who you are), [[character]] card, Scenario, Example dialogues, [[summary]], [[authornote]], and Chat History. Assignable globally, per character, or per [[chat-session]] via [[connections]].

terms.name: Macro
terms.desc: A placeholder in {{curly braces}} that gets automatically replaced with real content when Glaze builds the [[preset]] prompt. Common examples: {{char}} (character name), {{user}} (your name), {{description}}, {{scenario}}, {{random::a::b}} (random choice), {{roll::1d20}} (dice roll). Also works in [[regex]] replacement strings.

terms.name: Author's Note
terms.desc: A short note you can write separately for each [[chat-session]]. It's placed near the very end of the conversation in the AI's view, giving it strong influence over the next reply. Great for current plot reminders, style directions, or anything the AI should keep in mind right now.

terms.name: Guided Generation
terms.desc: Sends a one-time instruction alongside the next message to steer the AI's reply — for example, directing the plot, tone, or writing style. Also refers to the sampling settings that shape how the AI picks words: [[temperature]], [[top-p]], and similar parameters.

terms.name: Temperature
terms.desc: Controls how creative or predictable the AI's replies are. Low (0.1-0.5) = safe and focused, but can become repetitive. High (1.0-2.0) = varied and creative, but may turn incoherent. For roleplay, 0.7-1.2 is a good starting range.

terms.name: Top-P
terms.desc: Limits the pool of words the AI can pick from at each step. At 1.0, everything is fair game. At 0.9, it only considers the most likely 90% of words, cutting out rare and unusual choices. Lower values = more focused and predictable replies.

terms.name: Top-K
terms.desc: Limits the AI to the K most likely words at each step. For example, Top-K 40 keeps only the 40 highest-probability [[token]]s and discards the rest before sampling. 0 turns it off (no limit). Lower values make replies more focused; it works alongside [[temperature]] and [[top-p]].

terms.name: Frequency Penalty
terms.desc: Reduces repetition by penalizing words the more often they have already appeared. Positive values (up to 2.0) push the AI away from reusing the same words and phrasings; negative values encourage repetition. 0 is neutral. Only supported by some providers (OpenAI-style).

terms.name: Presence Penalty
terms.desc: Discourages the AI from reusing any word that has already appeared at all, regardless of how many times. Positive values (up to 2.0) push toward new topics and fresh vocabulary; negative values keep it on the same subjects. 0 is neutral. Only supported by some providers (OpenAI-style).

terms.name: Message Role
terms.desc: Each message in the conversation has a label that affects how the AI perceives it. 'system' — an instruction from the system, the AI treats it almost as a given. 'user' — triggers the model's user-interaction behavior patterns. 'assistant' — the model thinks it wrote this itself (prefill), and tends to repeat the style.

terms.name: Injection Point
terms.desc: Controls where a block appears in the list of messages sent to the AI. 'Relative' keeps it in its natural order among the blocks. 'Depth' inserts it a fixed number of messages before the end — for example, depth 2 places it just before the last 2 chat messages, giving it strong immediate influence. The Summary block has a third mode, 'In place of the messages': each run of summary blocks goes into the history where the messages it retells were, oldest first.

terms.name: Prompt Post-Processing
terms.desc: Reshapes the finished prompt right before it goes out, for endpoints that are picky about message structure. 'Merge consecutive roles' glues neighbouring messages that share a role into one — fewer, longer messages, which some models handle better. 'Semi-strict' additionally turns every system message after the first into a user message, so the conversation alternates. 'Strict' does the same and guarantees the prompt opens on a user message, inserting a filler turn if needed — this is what APIs like Anthropic's require. 'Single user message' folds the entire conversation into one message. Offered for custom endpoints only: every built-in protocol already normalizes whatever its wire format requires. Leave it on 'None' unless the endpoint complains.

terms.name: NoAssistant
terms.desc: A special mode that puts the entire conversation into one big block of text with 'User:' and 'Character:' labels, instead of sending separate messages. Helps reduce the model's predisposition toward the user. Requires a character card in a special format and third-person messages — the user must be hidden from the model.

terms.name: Stop String
terms.desc: A word or phrase that tells the AI to stop generating immediately when it writes that text. In NoAssistant mode, this prevents the AI from writing your character's lines — for example, adding 'User:' as a stop string makes the AI stop before it tries to reply on your behalf. Macros work here: '{{user}}:' becomes your persona's name followed by a colon.

terms.name: Reasoning
terms.desc: Some AI models 'think out loud' before giving their final answer, working through their reasoning step by step. 'Request Model Reasoning' only affects visibility and does not disable the model's thinking process. 'Parse Inline Reasoning' is made for cases when the model sends its thinking inside the response text rather than in a separate block — it extracts it from tags like <think>...</think> and displays it separately.

terms.name: Parse Inline Reasoning
terms.desc: Automatically extracts thinking/reasoning from the model's main message body and moves it to a separate UI block. This is especially useful for models like DeepSeek V3 that use tags like `<think>...</think>` instead of a dedicated reasoning field, and for presets designed to bypass native reasoning features by forcing the model to 'think out loud' directly in its response text.

terms.name: Show Native Reasoning
terms.desc: Enables display of the model's native [[preset-reasoning|reasoning]]. When turned off, Glaze does not store the model's reasoning. A local setting — it does not affect how the model works, only whether its thinking is kept and shown to you.

terms.name: Reasoning Effort
terms.desc: How much effort a reasoning-capable model puts into thinking before it answers. Higher levels (high, max) mean deeper, longer [[preset-reasoning|reasoning]] — usually better on hard tasks, but slower and more expensive. Lower levels (min, low) reply faster and cheaper. 'auto' lets the provider decide. Only affects models that support native reasoning.

terms.name: How the AI remembers a chat
terms.desc:
A model remembers nothing between requests: every time, the whole prompt is sent again — preset, card, lorebooks and the chat history. The history grows, the [[context|context window]] does not. Once it stops fitting, the oldest messages are simply cut off ([[history-trim|history trim]]) and the model no longer knows about them.

So the old parts are not lost, Glaze has two memory tools. They work independently and complement each other:

• [[summary|Summary]] — a continuous short retelling of the whole old chat. Always sent, in place of the messages it retells. Gives the model the thread of the story: who, where, what happened, where things stand.

• [[memorybook|Memory Books]] — a library of separate episodes. Only the entries that fit the current scene go into the prompt. Gives the model the details: what exactly was said, what the room looked like, what promise was made.

A simple rule: the summary is “what has happened so far”, Memory Books are “remember that moment”. [[lorebook|Lorebooks]] sit next to them but are something else: written by the author or by you, they hold facts about the world, not events of the chat.

Both tools are written by a separate model — the [[memory-connection|Memory slot]] connection. Everything is set up in the chat's Memory sheet.

terms.name: Summary
terms.desc:
A short retelling of the earlier parts of the chat, sent to the model instead of the messages themselves. The model remembers what happened, and the prompt does not bloat.

The summary is made of [[summary-block|blocks]]. Each block retells a run of consecutive old messages. While a block is in force, its messages are not sent — the retelling takes their place. In the chat the messages stay; nothing is deleted.

Blocks appear in two ways: [[summary-compact|by hand]] with “Compact history”, or [[summary-auto|automatically]] as the prompt fills up. Once there are many blocks, neighbouring ones are [[summary-merge|merged]] into broader ones, so the summary does not eat the context itself.

How to retell is up to the [[summary-prompts|summary prompts]]; where the finished text goes in the prompt is the [[summary-injection|injection point]]. The “Enabled” switch in the summary settings takes it out of the prompt without deleting the blocks.

Blocks can be read and edited, deleted (their messages go back into the prompt as written), regenerated, and you can add notes of your own.

terms.name: Summary block
terms.desc:
One part of the [[summary|summary]]: a retelling of a run of consecutive messages. The block's title is the numbers of the messages it replaces, e.g. “41-60”.

Levels. A level-1 block retells the messages themselves. Once there are many blocks, adjacent blocks of one level are [[summary-merge|merged]] into one block a level up. Merged blocks go to the archive: they are not sent, but if you delete the merged block, they come back.

Going stale. If a block's source messages are edited or deleted, the block is marked stale and stops being sent, and its messages go back into the prompt. It can be regenerated from the new text.

Drafts. “Regenerate” and “Shorten block” do not replace the text at once: the new version appears on the card as a draft, and you approve or discard it.

Notes. Your own text, added with “Note”. It is passed to the model only when messages are retold (as a hint of what matters); it is not sent with the chat request and is never merged.

Size. Every block shows how many tokens it has and how many it was made from. The desired length is the “Block size” setting.

terms.name: Manual history compaction
terms.alt: Compact history, Keep as written, Fresh history
terms.desc:
“Compact history” in the Memory sheet retells the old part of the chat into [[summary|summary]] blocks — one block per request, until it reaches the newest part. It runs in the background: the sheet can be closed, and finished blocks are saved as they land. “Stop compaction” finishes the block under way and stops.

The newest part is left alone. Its size is “Keep as written” in the “Compact history” button section: a share of the chat connection's context (25% by default) or a fixed number of tokens. The last two messages always stay. Everything older goes into the summary, and you can play on and compact again later.

“Nothing to compact” means the whole history outside the summary fits in that newest part. The note shows the numbers: how much history there is and how much is kept. Lower “Keep as written”, or press “Compact all but the newest messages” — it retells everything but the last two messages, whatever the setting says.

How much the button would retell right now is shown in the summary settings, under “This chat now”.

Manual compaction does not depend on [[summary-auto|auto compaction]]: it works with it off.

terms.name: Auto compaction
terms.alt: Compaction threshold, Compact down to, Least fresh history
terms.desc:
The automatic mode of the [[summary|summary]]. Off by default; applies to all chats at once.

How it works: after each bot reply Glaze checks how full the prompt is. If it is past the threshold, the oldest messages are retold into blocks until the prompt drops to the “Compact down to” line. It runs between turns, so one run takes at most 12 steps — the rest is done after the next replies.

Settings:

• Compaction threshold — how much of the room the prompt may use can fill before compaction starts. For example, 75%.

• Compact down to — how full to compact down to. This is the level of the whole prompt (preset, card, lorebooks, memory, summary and the history left), not a share of the history. No higher than the threshold. Set it lower and a run frees some headroom, so the next one does not start one turn later.

• Least fresh history — how many of the newest messages always stay as written, even when the preset and lorebooks take nearly all the room themselves.

“This chat now” shows where compaction would start and how much history it would leave. If “Compact down to” falls under the fixed part of the prompt, auto compaction can leave only the least — a warning appears there too.

terms.name: Merging and block size
terms.alt: Merge threshold, Block size, Shorten a large block
terms.desc:
The summary takes room too. To keep it from growing, there is merging: once all [[summary|summary]] blocks together take more than the “Merge threshold” (20% of the context by default), adjacent blocks of one level are merged into one a level up. Details of old events get smoothed over while recent ones stay sharper — the way human memory works. Merged blocks go to the archive and come back if the merged block is deleted. You can merge by hand: tick two or more adjacent blocks of one level and press “Merge selected”.

Block size is the desired length of one block in tokens (1000 by default). It is a ceiling: a short run of messages gives a shorter block, about a third of the source. Merging aims at this size too.

Models keep length in tokens poorly, so the prompt also gets the size in words and characters. If a block still comes out well past it, it is sent back once with the “Shorten a large block” prompt. A large block's card has a “Shorten block” button that does the same by hand.

If the model returns text no shorter than its source, the block is not saved and an error appears: lower the block size or change the model.

terms.name: Summary prompts
terms.alt: Retelling messages, Merging blocks, Refusal instruction
terms.desc:
The instructions the model follows to write the [[summary|summary]]. There are three, each with built-in presets, and you can save your own:

• Retelling messages — how to turn a run of messages into a block.
• Merging blocks — how to bring adjacent blocks into one a level up.
• Shortening a large block — how to cut down a block that came out too long.

[[macro|Macros]] work in your own prompts: {{char}}, {{user}}, {{getvar::…}} and special ones. {{target_tokens}}, {{target_words}} and {{target_chars}} place the size target in tokens, words and characters (if the prompt does not place them, the target in words and characters is appended). {{previous_summary}} places the blocks before the run being retold, so the model has the context. {{history}} places the transcript itself; a prompt that places it is sent as one message, as written. {{level}} places the level of the block a merge makes. The full list is under “Macros in prompts” in the settings.

The refusal instruction goes first in all three prompts. It is for models that refuse to retell harsh scenes: it asks to retell them neutrally, without detail, but leaving out nothing the story needs. Applies to all chats.

“Open current prompts” shows exactly what will go to the model now.

terms.name: Summary injection point
terms.desc:
Where the [[summary|summary]] text sits in the prompt. The setting is written into the Summary block of the current [[preset|preset]], so the section shows only when the preset has that block.

• In place of messages — each run of blocks goes into the history where the messages it retells were, oldest first. The most natural option: the model sees the retelling exactly where the conversation was.

• Relative — all of the summary as one piece where the Summary block sits in the preset.

• At depth — the given number of messages from the end of the history.

Role (System, User, Assistant) — who the model sees this message from. Usually System.

terms.name: Memory Books
terms.desc:
The chat's book of memories: a set of separate entries, each describing one episode — what happened in a given stretch of the conversation. Every chat has its own book.

An entry is a title, a text, keywords and the numbers of its source messages. It can also carry an importance and a “locked” mark.

Where entries come from. The model writes drafts from stretches of the conversation; you review and approve them — only then does a draft become an entry. You can also write an entry by hand. More in [[memorybook-drafts|Memory drafts]].

How they get into the prompt. Before every reply Glaze looks for entries that fit the current scene — by keywords and, with embeddings set up, by meaning. The best of them, as many as fit the budget, go into the prompt. More in [[memorybook-retrieval|Memory retrieval]], [[memorybook-budget|Budget and packing]] and [[memorybook-injection|Where memory goes]].

How it differs from the [[summary|summary]]: the summary is always sent and retells everything in order, briefly. Book entries sit in the library and come out only when relevant, but in more detail. They work well together: the summary keeps the story's thread, the book recalls the details.

What made it into the last request is shown in the context coverage card above the chat and in the [[request-preview|prompt inspector]].

terms.name: Memory drafts
terms.desc:
How [[memorybook|Memory Books]] entries come about.

The chat is cut into stretches of “Messages per draft”. For each stretch no memory covers yet, a draft is created. An empty draft is just a range of messages; the model writes a title, text and keys for it. A finished draft waits for you: approve it (it becomes an entry), edit it or discard it.

• Scan chat — find every uncovered stretch and create drafts. Handy for an old chat.

• Auto-create drafts — after every “Messages per draft” new messages, a draft is created by itself.

• Draft lag — how many of the newest messages to keep out of drafts. The last exchange is often edited or swiped; a lag of 2–4 messages lets you do that without regenerating memory.

• Auto-generate drafts — ask the model to fill new drafts at once. Off, drafts are created empty and wait until you press “Generate”.

• Batch size — how many drafts are generated in one go. Requests go out with a short pause so as not to hit the provider's limits.

Drafts are written by the [[memory-connection|Memory slot]] connection with the chosen memory generation prompt. If an entry's source messages change later, it is marked as needing a rebuild.

terms.name: Memory retrieval
terms.alt: Memory selection, Memory mode, Search query
terms.desc:
How Glaze decides which [[memorybook|Memory Books]] entries to put into this request.

1. The search query. Your current message and the latest turns of the chat (“Recent turns in search”), optionally the assistant's replies too (“Search assistant replies”). It is all cut to “Max search query characters”: less — sharper on the newest text, more — broader but blurrier.

2. Matches. By the entry's keywords: “Text only” looks for a key as a piece of text, “Glaze keys” as a separate word, “Text and keys” either way. With embeddings set up, also by meaning ([[embeddings|vector search]]): an entry fits if its similarity to the query is above the “Similarity threshold”.

3. Ranking. Candidates are sorted by relevance. You can add “Prefer recent memories” (a bonus for entries from recent messages; the “half-life” is how many messages it takes for the bonus to halve), “Prefer important memories” and “Avoid duplicates” (do not take many similar entries).

4. Filter. “Skip sources already visible” does not insert an entry whose messages are still in the prompt's history — no point repeating them.

5. Selection within the [[memorybook-budget|budget]].

The memory mode sets which signals are used: Legacy — a simple top-N pick; Fast — keys and vectors with modern ranking; Balanced — plus matches on entities, places and topics, emotion and importance; Deep — for now the same as Balanced. No mode makes extra requests to the model.

terms.name: Memory budget and packing
terms.desc:
How much room [[memorybook|memory]] may take in the prompt, and how entries are fitted in.

The budget is a share of the context (up to 35% by default) and, optionally, a hard ceiling “Max memory tokens in prompt”. The smaller of the two applies. “Max memories in prompt” caps the number of entries.

Packing decides what to do when the fitting entries do not fit:

• Full — whole entries only. Reliable, but fewer fit.
• Hybrid — whole entries while they fit; the rest of the budget is filled with excerpts of the entries that were cut.
• Chunks — entries are cut into pieces (by paragraph, up to “Tokens per chunk”), and the most relevant pieces from different entries go in, in the original order of events.

In Chunks mode, a few best entries (“Top entries”) first get their best pieces guaranteed — so something recent or found by meaning does not lose to old entries with lots of keyword hits. Then the rest of the budget is filled by overall ranking, no more than “Chunks per memory” from one entry.

“Compress large memories” — allow excerpts in place of whole entries when they do not fit.

terms.name: Where memory goes
terms.desc:
Where in the prompt the chosen [[memorybook|Memory Books]] entries end up.

• Hard block (default) — Glaze adds a separate “Memory Book” system message itself. Nothing to set up.

• {{memory}} — memory goes where the [[preset|preset]] has the {{memory}} [[macro|macro]] or a Memory Book block. That lets you place it where you want — say, inside your own tag next to the summary. If the preset has neither, memory is gathered but goes nowhere — a warning appears in the chat.

terms.name: Memory connection
terms.desc:
The model that writes the [[summary|summary]] and [[memorybook|Memory Books]] drafts. It is a separate Memory slot in the [[api|API]] settings, shared by both. When it is not set, the chat connection is used.

Memory does not need the strongest model: the job is to retell carefully, not to invent. A fast, cheap model with a large context usually fits best. If the model refuses to retell harsh scenes, turn on the refusal instruction in the [[summary-prompts|summary prompts]] or change the model.

Generation temperature — off: drafts are written at a low temperature; this is extracting facts, not prose. Output limit — off: taken from the connection; turn it on if the provider rejects the request (its ceiling counts reasoning tokens too).

terms.name: Embeddings
terms.desc:
A way to search by meaning rather than by exact words. A separate small model (an embedding model) turns text into a list of numbers — a vector. Texts with similar meaning get vectors close to each other, so “she burst into tears” is found by the query “crying” even though they share no words.

In Glaze, embeddings power search by meaning in [[memorybook|Memory Books]], in [[lorebook|lorebooks]] with vector entries, and search through old chat messages. Without them, all of these work by keywords only.

The embeddings connection is set up separately from the chat: the address, key and model of a provider that serves vectors. It is usually cheap, and one model serves every chat. After changing the model, always [[memorybook-reindex|reindex]] — vectors from different models are not compatible.

terms.name: MemoryBook Embedding Model
terms.desc: The model that converts MemoryBook entries and the retrieval query into numerical vectors for semantic search. Different embedding models create different, incompatible vector spaces. After changing the embedding model, you MUST run [[memorybook-reindex|Reindex]].

terms.name: Reindex MemoryBook
terms.desc: Recreates vectors for every active MemoryBook entry with the current [[memorybook-embedding-model|embedding model]]. Reindexing is mandatory after initial embedding setup and after every model change: old vectors are incompatible with the new model and can produce incorrect retrieval or ranking. Reindexing does not delete or rewrite memories; it only rebuilds their search index.

terms.name: Lorebook
terms.desc: A collection of information entries automatically added to the AI's memory when certain keywords appear in the chat. Think of it like a secret encyclopedia — when a place name, character name, or topic comes up, the relevant entry is silently included. Great for world details, [[character]] backstories, and lore. Control what triggers entries with [[lorebook-keys]] and how much space they use with [[lorebook-budget]].

terms.name: Primary / Secondary Keys
terms.desc: The keywords that trigger a lorebook entry. When a primary keyword appears in the recent chat, the entry activates. Secondary keys act as an extra filter: the entry only fires if those are present too. The exact combination logic — AND, OR, NOT — is set in [[lorebook-logic]]. To see which entries actually fired for a given message, check [[triggered-items]].

terms.name: Logic Mode
terms.desc: Controls how primary and secondary keywords combine to decide if an entry activates. 'Primary Only' — secondary keywords are ignored. 'AND Any/All' — secondary keywords must also be present. 'NOT Any/All' — the entry only fires if secondary keywords are absent.

terms.name: Context Percent / Budget Cap
terms.desc: Limits how much of the AI's memory lorebook entries can occupy. The AI can only hold so much text at once — this controls what share lorebooks are allowed to use. Context Percent sets a relative cap (e.g. 20%). Budget Cap sets a hard token limit. Entries are sorted by priority and added until the budget runs out.

terms.name: Probability
terms.desc: Even when an entry's keywords match, it only activates with this probability (0-100%). Use it to add randomness — for example, a 50% chance means a character's backstory is only included half the time their name appears.

terms.name: Sticky / Cooldown / Delay
terms.desc: Three timing controls for entries. Sticky: the entry stays active for N turns after its keywords stop appearing. Cooldown: after triggering, the entry won't fire again for N turns. Delay: the entry won't activate at all until N turns have passed in the chat.

terms.name: Group Scoring
terms.desc: Entries in the same named group compete: only the one with the highest weight activates, not all of them at once. Useful for mutually exclusive facts — for example, different weather descriptions for the same location.

terms.name: Recursive Scan
terms.desc: After adding lorebook entries to the AI's context, Glaze re-checks the newly added text for more keyword matches. This creates chains — one entry can trigger another, like a linked encyclopedia. Use with caution: it can cause loops where entries keep triggering each other.

terms.name: Regex Scripts
terms.desc: Special scripts that find text matching a specified pattern and replace it with a specified template. Control what kind of text it affects via [[regex-placement]]. To see which scripts were applied to a specific message, check [[triggered-items]].

terms.name: Placement
terms.desc: Controls which text the script runs on: 'User Input' (your messages before sending), 'AI Output' (the model's replies), 'World Info' (lorebook content), or 'Reasoning' (model thinking). A single script can target multiple text types at once.

terms.name: Ephemerality
terms.desc: 'Alter Chat Display' — only what you see on screen changes; the stored text and what the AI receives stay the same. 'Alter Outgoing Prompt' — the AI actually receives the modified version. Both options can be active at the same time.

terms.name: Trim Out
terms.desc: A list of strings (one per line) that are stripped from all regex matches before the replacement is applied. Useful for cleaning up unwanted characters that should always be removed, regardless of what triggered the match.

terms.name: Macros in Find Regex
terms.desc: Whether [[macro]] placeholders like {{char}} and {{user}} are expanded in the search pattern before matching. 'Don't substitute' — match the literal text {{char}}. 'Substitute raw' — replace with the actual character name first. 'Substitute escaped' — replace and escape special regex characters so they match literally.

terms.name: JanitorAI Extraction
terms.desc:
Janitor AI sits behind Cloudflare and never hands out a closed character card through its public API. Glaze works around this the way a browser would: it drives a hidden WebView carrying your signed-in Janitor.AI session, so every request passes Cloudflare exactly as it would in a real tab.

To recover a card, Glaze creates a throwaway proxy preset, opens a fresh chat with the character, sends a message and intercepts the generateAlpha response — the assembled prompt, which contains the character card wrapped in tags. The chat, the persona and the preset are removed again afterwards, and the account's generation settings are restored.

It needs “Extract JanitorAI cards with” set to Local in Settings, and a signed-in account. A character whose creator forbade proxies can never be captured: Janitor AI refuses to assemble its prompt at all, and only the public part of such a card can be imported. The same capture is what recovers closed lorebooks — see [[janitor-closed-lorebook]].

terms.name: Closed Lorebook Extraction
terms.desc:
Closed lorebooks are processed on the Janitor AI server, so pulling them out in their original form is impossible. As a workaround Glaze sends the character card, the catalog description and whatever else you picked into the chat. That text reaches the Janitor AI server, where it triggers lorebook entries; the server injects those entries into the prompt, Glaze intercepts the generateAlpha response and isolates the entries, discarding everything else.

After that you can do two things:
•  download the extracted content as a plain .txt file (no keys or rules);
•  send the entries to your active model — together with the card and the description as context — and have it build a proper [[lorebook]] for you.

If the character uses a generic lorebook (a universe lorebook, a sex-positions lorebook…), this method may not trigger every entry automatically. The only way to pull those is to type the keys yourself during entry collection; that same text is then also passed to the model during the build for extra context.

Several closed lorebooks are merged into a single one — the capture assembles the whole prompt at once, so their entries arrive mixed together with no way to tell which book each came from. See [[janitor-extract-context]] and [[lorebook-key-context]].

terms.name: Lorebook Build Prompt
terms.desc:
The system prompt your own model receives when it turns captured lorebook text into keyed World Info entries. It tells the model how to split the text into entries, what to write into content, key, keysecondary, comment and order, and to answer with JSON and nothing else.

There are two of them: one for text recovered from an assembled prompt (see [[janitor-closed-lorebook]]) and one for a scripted “advanced” lorebook, whose entries have to be recovered from JavaScript source instead. Both can be edited in the extraction settings (the gear in the Lorebooks sheet header); clearing a field restores the built-in prompt.

Edit it when your model needs firmer instructions — stricter JSON, a different language for the keys, fewer or larger entries. Keep the JSON contract intact: Glaze parses the answer as an entries array, so a prompt that stops asking for JSON produces a build that fails to parse. “Preview prompt” in the build stage shows exactly what will be sent, edits included.

terms.name: Extraction Context
terms.desc:
What Glaze stuffs into the message it sends into the Janitor AI chat to make the closed lorebook fire. Everything you select is concatenated into one latest user turn, so every keyword stays inside Janitor's scan depth. More text means more entries triggered — and a larger prompt.

The character card is the strongest trigger: it names the people, places and items the entries are keyed on. The catalog description and the scenario add public context, the first message(s) add the opening scene, and lorebook descriptions add the book's own summary. Custom text is where you type keys the character never says on its own — the only way to reach entries of a generic or universe lorebook. Tap a source to see the exact text it sends and its token count.

This is a different choice from [[lorebook-key-context]], which is about what the model reads afterwards. See [[janitor-closed-lorebook]].

terms.name: Context for Key Inference
terms.desc:
Extraction returns the lorebook's text, not its trigger keys — those stay on the Janitor AI server and are never sent. The build model has to infer them, and this is the context it gets to do it with: the character card, the catalog description, the scenario, the first message(s), the descriptions of the attached lorebooks and any notes of your own.

It is only read, never written back: nothing selected here becomes an entry. It only shapes the [[lorebook-keys]] the model assigns to the entries that were recovered, so sources naming the same people and places as the entries give noticeably better keys. The selection you made for [[janitor-extract-context]] is carried over here after the extraction, and you can change it before building.

terms.name: Themes
terms.desc: Customize how the app looks. Switch between light and dark mode, change the accent color, set custom colors for message bubbles, pick fonts for the UI and chat, and control the transparency and blur of background elements. Theme settings apply globally across all chats.
